blocks.x: Circuit-based ML and chemistry simulation with verification-first rigor: trainability screens before training runs, noise-aware benchmarks that survive real hardware, classical surrogates as the honest control — and sim-to-real validation before any claim ships.
Trainability is discovered on paper, not after the GPU bill

Quantum ML and simulation are research lanes with real engineering discipline: variational circuits for kernels and generative tasks, Hamiltonian simulation for chemistry and materials. The honest posture is dual-track — the quantum track builds benchmarked capability, and the classical track builds the surrogates that do today's work while hardware matures.

Verification is the whole game: simulator-to-hardware agreement, error-aware metrics, and comparison against the best classical methods (which are better than most demos admit). Where quantum shows signal, the ledger records it; the classical surrogate fleet keeps shipping value regardless.
Below: the failure modes that seduce quantum-ML programs, the reference architecture of the verification pipeline, and the console that tracks hardware agreement.
Four ways quantum-ML programs get seduced
Each of these produces a notebook result that evaporates on real hardware — the countermeasures screen trainability, respect noise and keep the classical surrogate honest.
